pins.title: Escríbelo. Dilo en voz alta: write it down in Spanish, then say it out loud
pins.description:
Here's a small habit for learning Spanish at home. Write a sentence or two about your day in Spanish, then read them out loud. Writing gives you time to find the words, and saying them makes them easier to reach in a real conversation. The Dime Más Journal, made to use alongside the cards, is coming soon.

pins.title: Which language would you learn next? More than 7,000 are spoken around the world
pins.description:
More than 7,000 languages are in use around the world today, according to Ethnologue. Every one of them is a way into someone's life. Which one would you learn next, and who would you most like to talk to in it? Ask it at dinner or at your next language exchange and listen to the reasons people give.

pins.title: Which meal tastes like a place to you?
pins.description:
A question about food and memory. It might be something you ate once, somewhere you'd never been before, or toast at your nan's kitchen table. Ask a friend this one and you'll usually get a story along with the answer.

Free printable: 20 questions to start a real conversation in Spanish, at profluency.co.uk

pins.title: The best conversations start with a pause: a simple listening tip
pins.description:
After you ask a question, there's a small quiet while the other person decides how much to tell you. Don't rush to fill it. Give them a moment and the real answer usually comes. It's one of the easiest ways to have deeper conversations with friends, and it helps in a new language too.

Free printable: 20 questions to start a real conversation in Spanish, at profluency.co.uk

pins.title: Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres: a Spanish saying about the company you keep
pins.description:
Dime con quién andas y te diré quién eres means “tell me who you spend time with, and I'll tell you who you are”. It's close to the English “birds of a feather”. In Spain it's often a warning about the company you keep, though friends use it to tease each other too. Try it when a friend starts sounding just like their flatmate.

pins.title: Hoy recordamos contando historias: All Saints' Day in Spain and Día de Muertos in Mexico
pins.description:
Hoy recordamos contando historias means “today, we remember by telling stories”. In Spain, 1 November is el Día de Todos los Santos, when families take flowers to the cemetery and bakeries sell huesos de santo. In Mexico, families build an ofrenda for el Día de Muertos, with photos and the favourite food of the people they miss. Whose story would you tell?

pins.title: Who made you feel at home somewhere new?
pins.description:
A question about belonging. Think of a neighbour who knocked with a plate of food, or a colleague who explained the rules nobody writes down. They probably don't know how much it mattered. Ask a friend this one, and if you can, tell that person too.

pins.title: Lean in. Ask the second question: a tip for better conversations
pins.description:
The first question is polite. The second one shows you were listening. Try a follow-up like “What was that like?” or “And then what happened?” In Spanish you can simply say “dime más”, tell me more. Try it once this week and notice how much more you hear.

Free printable: 20 questions to start a real conversation in Spanish, at profluency.co.uk
